fixes.fix: Teeth are not bone, and they do not regenerate.
fixes.was: Enamel is the hardest substance in the body — harder than bone — but once it's gone the body cannot rebuild it. That's the entire reason fluoride, sealants and restoratives exist.
— written "Banko." The Big 3 are Henry Schein, Patterson, Benco.

fixes.fix: Envista · Dentsply Sirona · Straumann · Invisalign · Planmeca
fixes.was: — the notes have In Vista, Dens Supply Cerona, Sventum/Staman, Invisilin, Plan Mecha.

cards.q: Largest dental distributor in the world?
cards.a: Henry Schein — roughly 40% of the market. #1.
cards.n: Your notes spell it "Henry Shine."

cards.q: Who are the Big 3 distributors, in order?
cards.a:
1. Henry Schein (~40%)
  2. Patterson
  3. Benco
cards.n: Notes say "Banko" — it's Benco.

cards.q: What role does the distributor play in a dental office?
cards.a: The quarterback — everything the office runs on comes through them.

cards.q: How are dental distributor reps typically employed?
How does Henry Schein get devices to the office?
cards.a: Ships all dental devices straight to the door.

cards.q: Roughly how many dentist products are out there?
Who are the largest dental manufacturers?
cards.a: Envista, Dentsply Sirona, Straumann.
cards.n: Notes: "In Vista / Dens Supply Cerona / Sventum."

cards.q: Which implant companies does Henry Schein own?
cards.a: BioHorizons and Camlog — its implant arm.
cards.n: Straumann is the big independent implant player.

cards.q: Which two companies sell dental equipment and technology?
cards.a: A-dec and Planmeca.
cards.n: Notes: "Plan Mecha."

cards.q: Newest way to take x-rays?
cards.a: The intraoral scanner.

cards.q: Why do dentists think about money differently than surgeons and physicians?
cards.a: Surgeons and physicians are on salary. Dentists make what they charge their patients — so every purchase is their own money.

cards.q: What is dental insurance really?
cards.a: Not insurance — more of a discount program.

cards.q: How does Medicaid work in dental?
cards.a: It doesn't. Medicaid covers the uninsured and people on welfare on the medical side; dental has no equivalent.

cards.q: Which procedures are normally out of pocket?
cards.a: Dentures, crowns, veneers.

cards.q: Roughly how many dentists are there in the world?
What do the letters DMD after a name tell you?
cards.a: A typical dentist — a general practitioner.

cards.q: Name the dental specialists.
cards.a:
• Orthodontists
  • Endodontists
  • Pedodontists
  • Periodontists
  • Oral surgeons

cards.q: Biggest clear aligner company in the game?
cards.a: Invisalign.
cards.n: Notes: "Invisilin."

cards.q: What are the Big 4 procedure categories?
cards.a:
1. Implants
  2. Preventives
  3. Restoratives
  4. Endodontics

cards.q: Maxilla — what is it, and what's its one job?
cards.a: The upper jaw. Softer ground. Supports the upper teeth — and the sinus is right nearby.

cards.q: Mandible — what is it, and what's its one job?
cards.a: The lower jaw. Stronger ground. Supports the lower teeth and contains an important nerve.

cards.q: Gingiva — what is it, and what's its one job?
cards.a: The gums. A protective seal. Keeps bacteria away and protects the tooth and bone.

cards.q: Alveolar bone — what is it, and what's its one job?
cards.a: The foundation. Holds the tooth — and shrinks if the tooth is lost.
cards.n: That shrinking is why bone grafts get sold alongside implants.

cards.q: Trace the structure from the jaw out to the tooth.
cards.a: Jaw bone (maxilla or mandible) → alveolar bone → gums → teeth.

cards.q: Incisors, canines, premolars, molars — what does each one do?
cards.a:
1. Incisors — cut
  2. Canines — tear
  3. Premolars — crush
  4. Molars — grind

cards.q: Are teeth bone? Do they grow back?
cards.a: No and no. Teeth aren't bone. Enamel is the hardest substance in the body, but once it's lost the body can't rebuild it.
cards.n: Your notes say teeth are the hardest bone and the only bone that regenerates — both are wrong, and a dentist will catch it. The fact that enamel can't come back is what sells fluoride, sealants and restoratives.

cards.q: Why bother learning tooth composition at all?
cards.a: So you can talk about products that interact with each layer — that's the whole point of the anatomy.

cards.q: Cavities — what does the dentist buy?
cards.a:
1. Composite filling
  2. Bonding agents
  3. Caries detection devices
  4. Fluoride
  5. Sealants

cards.q: Periodontal disease — what does the dentist buy?
cards.a:
1. Ultrasonic scalers
  2. Hand scalers
  3. Lasers
  4. Bone grafts
  5. Antimicrobials

cards.q: Crooked teeth — what does the dentist buy?
cards.a:
1. Braces
  2. Clear aligners
  3. Temporary anchoring devices (TADs)
  4. Orthognathic surgery, in severe cases

cards.q: Losing teeth — what does the dentist buy?
cards.a:
1. Implant systems
  2. Bone grafts
  3. Dentures
  4. Digital dentures
  5. Implant components

cards.q: What are your odds the dentist is actually available when you walk in?
cards.a: About a 30% hit rate.

cards.q: How many touches before you get consistent calls?
Dentists are very ___ driven.
cards.a: Promo and sell driven.

cards.q: How do you build a relationship in this business?
cards.a: Show up. Be consistent. Bring value.

cards.q: Three things that keep a dentist calling you back?
cards.a:
1. Consistency
  2. Follow up
  3. Say what you'll actually do

cards.q: What matters most in dental sales?
cards.a: Relationships. They're the major thing.

cards.q: How many incisors, and where?
cards.a: 8 — 4 upper, 4 lower. Central and lateral.
cards.n: Single root, thin edge. Built for cutting.

cards.q: How many canines, and what else are they called?
cards.a: 4 — the "cuspids" or "eye teeth".

cards.q: How many premolars, and what else are they called?
cards.a: 8 — the "bicuspids".
cards.n: Bi-cuspid = two cusps. That's literally the name.

cards.q: How many molars?
cards.a: 12 — or 8 once the wisdom teeth come out.

cards.q: Which teeth have the longest roots in the mouth?
cards.a: Canines.
cards.n: Which is why they're very stable and the last teeth to be lost.

cards.q: How many cusps does a molar have?
cards.a: 3 to 5, with 2–3 roots. The largest teeth in the mouth.

cards.q: When do the first molars come in?
cards.a: Around age 6 — that's why they're called the "6-year molars".

cards.q: Where do premolars sit, and what do they do?
cards.a: Between the canines and molars. They're the transition — chewing and grinding. One or two roots.

cards.q: The team analogy for the four tooth types?
cards.a:
1. Incisors — skilled forwards (finesse, visible, aesthetic)
  2. Canines — anchors (stability, guidance)
  3. Premolars — midfielders (transition, support)
  4. Molars — power players (heavy lifting, most force)
cards.n: Straight from the training. Handy if you need to explain teeth to a patient.

cards.q: Which jaw has denser bone?
cards.a: The mandible — densest in the mouth, especially at the front. The maxilla is less dense.
cards.n: Density drives almost everything else: implant stability, how fast teeth move.

cards.q: Which jaw moves teeth faster in orthodontics, and why?
cards.a: The maxilla — thinner bone means faster movement. The lower jaw is slower.

cards.q: What's inside the maxilla that matters for implants?
cards.a: The maxillary sinuses.
cards.n: Not enough bone between the sinus and the mouth means a sinus lift before an upper back implant.

cards.q: What shape is the mandible, and what runs through it?
cards.a: Horseshoe shaped, with the mental foramen — the nerve exit — sitting between the premolars.

cards.q: What does healthy gingiva look like?
cards.a: Pink, stippled, and it doesn't bleed.
cards.n: Diseased: red, swollen, bleeds easily. Stippled means a slight orange-peel texture.

cards.q: What is gingiva made of?
cards.a: Keratinized tissue around the teeth — free gingiva and attached gingiva.

cards.q: What happens to alveolar bone once a tooth is gone?
cards.a: It resorbs — the bone disappears because nothing is stimulating it.
cards.n: "Use it or lose it." This one fact drives ridge preservation grafts, immediate placement, and half the implant conversation.

cards.q: How much bone can be lost after a tooth comes out?
cards.a: 40–60% in the first three years.
cards.n: Which is why timing matters so much — wait too long and there's nothing left to place an implant into.

cards.q: What actually causes a cavity?
cards.a: Streptococcus mutans + sugar → acid, and the acid demineralizes enamel.

cards.q: How does decay progress?
cards.a: White spot → enamel caries → dentin caries → pulp involvement.
cards.n: Catch it at the white spot and it's preventive. Let it reach the pulp and it's a root canal.

cards.q: Caries Class I and II?
cards.a:
Class I — pits and fissures on chewing surfaces.
Class II — between the back teeth.

cards.q: Caries Class III, IV and V?
cards.a:
Class III — between the front teeth.
Class IV — front teeth involving the corner or edge.
Class V — at the gumline.
cards.n: Class VI is cusp tips.

cards.q: What are healthy gums, by the numbers?
cards.a: 1–3mm pocket depth, no bleeding on probing, no bone loss.

cards.q: Gingivitis vs periodontitis?
cards.a:
Gingivitis is reversible — gums inflamed, bleeding, but no bone loss yet.
Periodontitis is irreversible — 4mm+ pockets and bone loss visible on x-ray.
cards.n: The line between them is bone loss. Once bone is gone it doesn't come back on its own.

cards.q: What causes gingivitis?
cards.a: Plaque accumulation. It's reversible at this stage.

cards.q: Angle's Class I?
cards.a: Normal molar relationship — but with crowding, spacing or other issues. The most common.

cards.q: Angle's Class II?
cards.a: Lower jaw too far back relative to the upper — overbite/overjet, the "buck teeth" look.
cards.n: Division 1: front teeth protrusive. Division 2: front teeth retroclined.

cards.q: Angle's Class III?
cards.a: Lower jaw too far forward — underbite. Can be dental or skeletal, and it's the hardest to treat.

cards.q: Partial vs complete edentulism?
cards.a:
Partial — missing some teeth. Bridges, partial dentures, implants.
Complete — no teeth in the arch. Complete dentures, implant-supported dentures, All-on-4.
cards.n: Partial edentulism gets sorted by Kennedy Classification (I–IV) based on where the gaps are.

cards.q: What happens to someone after they lose teeth?
cards.a: Bone resorption, bite collapse, facial aging, functional impairment.
cards.n: It's not just cosmetic — the face structurally changes as the bone goes.

cards.q: Why do incisors matter commercially?
cards.a: They're the most visible teeth, so aesthetics are critical — shade matching for composites, bonding and veneers, and aligner cases often focus here.
cards.n: Also trauma-prone in contact sports, which matters if the practice sees athletes.

cards.q: Why are canines strong implant candidates?
cards.a: Bone volume. They're also critical for "canine guidance" in the bite and strategic in denture and partial design.
cards.n: An impacted canine means complex orthodontic treatment.

cards.q: Why are premolars often extracted?
cards.a: To create space for orthodontic treatment.
cards.n: They're also a common site for cracked tooth syndrome, and implant-friendly locations.

cards.q: Why do molars drive so much product?
cards.a: Highest decay rate — grooves and pits mean sealants. Most common location for crowns, most complex root canal anatomy, and implants there need more bone because the forces are higher.

cards.q: Which teeth are usually impacted or extracted?
cards.a: Wisdom teeth — #1, 16, 17 and 32.

cards.q: Where's the best place to put an implant, and why?
cards.a: The mandible — dense bone. It also supports implant-retained dentures well.
cards.n: Upper back implants are harder: sinus lifts, slower stability, tougher for immediate load.

cards.q: What product category does the mandibular nerve create?
cards.a: Imaging. Nerve management is critical down there, so the practice needs to see exactly where it runs before placing.

cards.q: What sells off gum disease?
cards.a: Soft tissue lasers, periodontal instruments, grafting materials for recession, and tissue management during impressions.

cards.q: Two product names worth knowing?
cards.a:
DIAGNOdent — caries detection.
Arestin — local antimicrobial for perio.

cards.q: When does a ridge preservation graft get placed?
cards.a: At extraction — before the bone has a chance to resorb.
cards.n: Implants help maintain bone too. That's the argument for immediate placement.

cards.q: What's the ROI pitch on periodontal maintenance?
cards.a: Perio maintenance patients are recurring revenue for the practice.
cards.n: Selling the business case, not just the product.

cards.q: What's the biggest opportunity area, and why?
cards.a: Edentulism — the population is aging and the baby boomers are hitting peak tooth-loss years.
cards.n: Implant systems, bone grafting, dentures, digital denture workflow.

cards.q: Three questions to actually open with?
cards.a:
1. "What percentage of your restorations are composite vs amalgam these days?"
  2. "What percentage of your Class II cases do you treat with aligners vs traditional braces?"
  3. "The baby boomers are hitting peak tooth-loss years — how is your practice positioned to capture this?"
cards.n: Straight from the training. Each one gets a dentist talking about their own practice instead of your catalog.

fixes.fix: Nobel Biocare, Ormco and KaVo Kerr belong to Envista, not Danaher.
fixes.was: Your notes list them under both. Envista was spun off from Danaher and took the dental brands with it - saying "Danaher owns Nobel Biocare" to a rep who works there will land badly.

fixes.fix: It's Brånemark who invented the modern implant.
fixes.was: Worth being able to say the name - it comes up constantly in implant education, and Nobel Biocare's whole identity rests on it.

cards.q: What are orthodontists actually trained to do?
cards.a: Move teeth. That's the specialty.
cards.n: When Invisalign launched they only let orthodontists use it. If you ever need aligners yourself, go to an orthodontist.

cards.q: What happens if one person in the practice doesn't like you?
cards.a: Nobody will. The staff are extremely tight-knit — word travels instantly.
cards.n: Which is why the office manager and the assistants matter as much as the doctor.

cards.q: What should you do right after closing a sale?
cards.a: Ask when they plan to use it, put it on your calendar, and text them afterward to ask how it went.
cards.n: Turns one transaction into a relationship. Costs you nothing.

cards.q: Which orthodontic items are the repeat business?
cards.a: Wires, ligature rings and rubber bands. Brackets are bonded on and painful to change, so they're the hard sell.
cards.n: Sell the consumable that gets replaced, not the one that stays put.

cards.q: Inside vs outside sales rep?
cards.a:
Inside works the phones — straight cold calls.
Outside covers the territory in person, walking into practices.

cards.q: What share of a practice's spend goes to supplies?
cards.n: Small slice of their budget — which is why convenience and reliability often beat price.

cards.q: How much of the consumables market runs through full-service dealers?
cards.a: 80% — Henry Schein, Patterson and Benco.

cards.q: What does a full-service dealer actually offer?
cards.a:
• One-stop shopping (10,000+ SKUs)
  • A rep who visits regularly
  • Equipment and consumables
  • Practice management support
  • Financing

cards.q: What's your job if you work for a dealer?
cards.a:
1. Territory management — 50 to 150 practices
  2. Relationship building (know the office manager)
  3. Problem solving — emergency orders, back-orders
  4. Equipment referrals to specialists

cards.q: How is manufacturer-direct selling different?
cards.a: Specialized products (implants, lasers, specific tech), higher margins, more clinical education required.
cards.n: You're the expert on YOUR product; the dealer rep is a generalist across 10,000.

cards.q: Who are the discount suppliers, and why do they matter?
cards.a: Net32, DentalBuyer, Amazon Business. Price-focused, no service — a real threat to the traditional model.

cards.q: How do you compete with a discounter on price?
cards.a: You don't. Value-added service, emergency availability, and the practice relationship.
cards.n: You can't win a race to the bottom against Amazon. Don't enter it.

cards.q: What actually drives consumables purchases?
cards.a:
1. Reliability — "I need it tomorrow, can you deliver?"
  2. Price — but not always #1
  3. Consistency batch to batch
  4. Ease of ordering — portals, auto-ship
  5. Support — clinical questions, product issues

cards.q: What does the weekly or bi-weekly visit look like?
cards.a: Check inventory with the office manager, take orders, address product issues, introduce new products, and gather competitive intelligence — what are they buying elsewhere?

cards.q: What happens monthly vs quarterly?
cards.a:
Monthly: deeper account review, lunch for the staff, volume discounts, contract renewals.
Quarterly: practice growth planning, equipment needs assessment, large capital discussions.

cards.q: Which numbers do you track on an account?
cards.a:
1. Monthly purchase volume
  2. Product mix — your brand vs competitors
  3. Growth rate
  4. Order frequency
  5. Average order size

cards.q: How is selling equipment different from consumables?
cards.a:
• $5,000 to $500,000+
  • Months, not days
  • Multiple stakeholders — owner, associates, office manager, lead assistant
  • Financing almost always involved
  • ROI has to be proven
  • Installation and training
  • Service contracts = recurring revenue

cards.q: The athletic parallel for a capital sale?
cards.a: "Like recruiting a star player. Long courtship, big investment, transformative impact, and everyone weighs in on the decision."

cards.q: Intraoral sensors — what, how much, how long?
cards.a:
Digital replacement for film. Instant image, lower radiation. Sizes 0 (pedo), 1 (anterior), 2 (posterior).
$5,000–12,000 per operatory, 2–4 month sales cycle.
cards.n: Wired vs wireless is a trade-off between cost, reliability and freedom.

cards.q: Who makes intraoral sensors?
cards.a: Dexis (KaVo Kerr / Danaher), Schick (Dentsply Sirona), Carestream.

cards.q: ROI pitch on digital x-ray?
cards.a:
1. No more film costs — $50–100/month
  2. Faster workflow, no developing
  3. Patient education, images chairside
  4. No chemicals
  5. Lower radiation is a marketing advantage

cards.q: Panoramic x-ray — the basics?
cards.a: Whole mouth and jaw in one image. 2D, or 3D with CBCT. $20,000–80,000. Planmeca, Carestream, Vatech.
cards.n: Used for implant planning, wisdom teeth, TMJ and orthodontics.

cards.q: CBCT — why is it a game-changer?
cards.a: 3D imaging — you can see bone in three dimensions. Becoming standard of care for implants. $60,000–150,000, 6–12 month sales cycle.

cards.q: CBCT ROI?
cards.a:
1. Refer fewer cases out — keep surgical implants in-house
  2. Better case acceptance — patients see 3D
  3. Avoid anatomical complications
  4. $200–400 scan fee per case
cards.n: Insurance coverage is limited, so it's often cash pay.

cards.q: Intraoral scanners — who are the players?
cards.a:
• iTero (Align) — integrates with Invisalign
  • TRIOS (3Shape)
  • Medit
  • Primescan (Dentsply Sirona) — integrates with CEREC
$20,000–40,000.
cards.n: Note who owns what — the integration angle is usually the whole pitch.

cards.q: Intraoral scanner ROI?
cards.a: No impression materials ($200–400/month), fewer remakes, no gagging, digital file to the lab instantly, Invisalign integration, and in-office milling with CAD/CAM.

cards.q: Best way to sell a scanner?
cards.a: Demo it in their office, on a real patient. Sales cycle 3–6 months.
cards.n: Nobody buys a $30k scanner off a brochure.

cards.q: What is CEREC?
cards.a: Dentsply Sirona's in-office CAD/CAM — the market leader. Mills crowns same day. Scanner + design software + milling unit, $100,000–150,000 complete.
cards.n: Ceramic blocks to mill run $30–80 each.

cards.q: CEREC ROI, and where's break-even?
cards.a: Same-day dentistry — no temporaries, no second visit. Eliminates lab fees of $150–300 per crown. Break-even around 150–200 crowns.
cards.n: Learning curve is 3–6 months to proficiency; sales cycle 6–12 months.

cards.q: CAD/CAM alternatives to CEREC?
cards.a: Planmeca PlanMill, Roland DWX, Straumann CARES.

cards.q: Digital dentures?
cards.a: Milled instead of made by traditional lab process. Growing fast — AvaDent and others. Straight at the aging-population opportunity.

cards.q: Soft tissue lasers?
cards.a: Frenectomies, gingivectomies, crown lengthening. Diode is most common. $5,000–15,000. Biolase (Epic), AMD Lasers, Fotona.

cards.q: Soft tissue laser ROI?
cards.a: Adds billable procedures, less bleeding, faster healing, and "laser dentistry" markets well.
cards.n: Insurance coverage is limited — mostly fee-for-service, which means the practice keeps more.

cards.q: Hard tissue lasers?
cards.a: Can cut tooth structure — replacing the drill for some procedures. Erbium (Er:YAG). $40,000–80,000, steeper learning curve, marketed hard as "no drill dentistry."

cards.q: How do you sell a laser?
cards.a: Demo or trial period is critical. Include CE course training, show clinical cases, bring marketing support materials.

cards.q: Autoclaves — what do you need to know?
cards.a: Steam sterilization. Class B (vacuum, most thorough), Class N, Class S. 6L / 8L / 12L+. $3,000–15,000. Midmark (Ritter), Tuttnauer, SciCan.
cards.n: Replacement cycle is every 7–10 years — which tells you when to call.

cards.q: Sales angle on an autoclave?
cards.a:
1. Regulatory compliance — it's required by law
  2. Cycle time — faster is more efficient
  3. Reliability — downtime means they can't practice

cards.q: Dental chairs?
cards.a: The centerpiece of the operatory. $6,000–20,000+ each. A-dec (premium), Midmark, Forest.
cards.n: Often tied to an office renovation, and financing is almost always required.

cards.q: Handpieces?
cards.a: High-speed runs 400,000 RPM — that's "the drill." Slow-speed is 20,000 RPM for prophy angles and adjustments. Electric or air-driven. $800–3,000 each.
cards.n: They keep 2–4 per operatory for sterilization rotation. KaVo, NSK, W&H.

cards.q: Compressors and suction?
cards.a: The compressor supplies air to the handpieces — $3,000–30,000, sized by number of chairs. No air means no drilling, so reliability is everything. Suction evacuates saliva and water.
cards.n: Quiet compressor models are a premium feature. Suction is usually bundled into a new office buildout.

cards.q: How big is the implant market, and why is it growing?
cards.a:
~$5 billion and growing.
  1. Baby boomers losing teeth
  2. Implants are now standard of care over bridges and dentures
  3. More GPs placing them, not just oral surgeons
  4. Success rates above 95%
  5. Digital workflow makes planning easier

cards.q: What are the three parts of an implant?
cards.a:
1. Fixture — the screw in the bone
  2. Abutment — connects crown to fixture
  3. Crown — the tooth-coloured part you see

cards.q: Fixture specs worth knowing?
cards.a: Titanium or zirconia. Diameters 3–6mm, lengths 6–18mm, platform mini / regular / wide.
cards.n: Surface treatment is the critical bit — it's what drives osseointegration.

cards.q: Which surface treatment belongs to which brand?
cards.a:
• SLA (sand-blasted, acid-etched) — Straumann
  • TiUnite — Nobel Biocare
  • Osseospeed — Astra Tech

cards.q: Abutment options?
cards.a: Stock or custom. Titanium or zirconia (white, for aesthetics). Straight or angled. Scanbodies are used for digital impressions.

cards.q: Straumann — the numbers?
cards.a:
~20% market share, #1. Swiss precision, premium pricing, deep evidence base. Roxolid (titanium-zirconium alloy — smaller diameter, same strength), BLT and BLX tapered lines.
$250–400 per implant to the dentist; the dentist charges the patient $2,000–4,000+.
cards.n: That spread is why cost usually isn't the surgeon's first question.

cards.q: Nobel Biocare?
cards.a: The pioneers — Brånemark invented the modern implant. All-on-4 is their trademark protocol (full arch on four implants). NobelActive is known for primary stability. Premium priced.

cards.q: Dentsply Sirona's implant line?
cards.a: Astra Tech — strong reputation for bone preservation, conical connection, and it integrates with CEREC for the digital workflow.

cards.q: Zimmer Biomet and BioHorizons?
cards.a:
Zimmer Biomet — Tapered Screw-Vent, popular in the US, value pricing, broad portfolio.
BioHorizons — US-based, Laser-Lok surface, growing in the GP market.

cards.q: The value implant brands?
cards.a: Hiossen, MegaGen, Dentium — $80–150 per implant versus $250–400 premium.
cards.n: The controversy is quality vs cost. The opportunity is price-sensitive practices and high-volume DSOs.

cards.q: What does the implant sales cycle look like?
cards.a:
3 to 12 months:
  1. Awareness — lunch-and-learn at the practice
  2. Education — CE course, often free and manufacturer-sponsored
  3. Trial — place a few cases with your support
  4. Conversion — they gain confidence
  5. Loyalty — and once trained, they rarely switch

cards.q: Why are implant systems so "sticky"?
cards.a:
1. Instruments and surgical kits are system-specific and expensive
  2. There's a learning curve to switch
  3. Compatibility issues
cards.n: Which cuts both ways — hard to win an account, very hard to lose one.

cards.q: What's your actual role in implant sales?
cards.a: Clinical educator — attend surgeries and provide guidance. Help plan difficult cases. Solve problems when things go wrong. Manage inventory so emergency implants are available.

cards.q: What drives the decision on an implant system?
cards.a: Clinical outcomes, ease of use, prosthetic flexibility, your availability when they need you, and the research evidence.
cards.n: Cost is often not #1 for surgeons — don't lead with price.

cards.q: Why does anyone need a bone graft?
cards.a: Extraction means the bone resorbs, and implants need adequate bone volume and density.
cards.n: Three situations: socket preservation right after extraction, sinus lifts for upper posterior implants, and ridge augmentation on deficient sites.

cards.q: What are the four types of graft?
cards.a:
1. Autograft — the patient's own bone
  2. Allograft — cadaver bone
  3. Xenograft — animal, usually bovine
  4. Alloplast — synthetic
cards.n: Auto, allo, xeno, allo-plast: self, human, animal, synthetic.

cards.q: Autograft — pros and cons?
cards.a: The patient's own bone, from chin, jaw or hip. Gold standard for integration — but it needs a second surgical site, which means added morbidity.

cards.q: Allograft?
cards.a: Processed, sterilized cadaver bone. LifeNet, MTF, AlloSource. Cancellous chips or cortical blocks, $100–500 per case.
cards.n: Popular because there's no second surgical site and it's readily available.

cards.q: Xenograft?
cards.a: Animal-derived, usually bovine. Bio-Oss (Geistlich) is the market leader. Acts as a scaffold for the patient's own bone to grow into, and resorbs slowly so it maintains volume. $150–400.

cards.q: Alloplast?
cards.a: Synthetic — hydroxyapatite, calcium phosphate. Novabone, Cerasorb. Unlimited supply and no disease transmission risk.

cards.q: What are membranes for?
cards.a: They cover the graft to guide tissue regeneration. Resorbable or not — collagen (Bio-Gide by Geistlich, Cytoplast) versus PTFE, which is non-resorbable and has to be removed. $30–200 each.

cards.q: The sales angle on grafting?
cards.a: Every extraction is a potential graft. Higher implant success with adequate bone, better patient comfort, and it's billable revenue for the practice.

cards.q: How dominant is Invisalign?
cards.a: ~90% of the clear aligner market. Made by Align Technology.

cards.q: How does an Invisalign case actually run?
cards.a:
1. Digital scan — iTero preferred
  2. AI treatment planning in ClinCheck
  3. Aligners manufactured centrally
  4. Shipped to the practice
  5. Patient wears 20–40+ sequentially, changing every 1–2 weeks

cards.q: Invisalign economics?
cards.a: $1,500–2,000 per case to the dentist. The patient pays $3,500–8,000. The dentist submits cases and pays per case.

cards.q: Where do aligners win, and where do they fall down?
cards.a:
Win: nearly invisible, removable for eating and brushing, digital and predictable, fewer office visits.
Fall down: complex cases are harder, compliance is critical (22 hrs/day), and they can't fix severe skeletal discrepancies.

cards.q: Who competes with Invisalign?
cards.a: ClearCorrect (Straumann-owned), SureSmile (Dentsply Sirona), uLab, Spark (Ormco). Usually 20–30% cheaper.

cards.q: Where's the growth in aligners?
cards.a: GPs doing more ortho now that aligners made it accessible, a growing teen market, and adults — who are over half of the aligner market.

cards.q: Brackets?
cards.a: Metal or ceramic (aesthetic), self-ligating or conventional. Ormco, 3M Unitek, American Orthodontics. $5–20 each.

cards.q: Wires?
cards.a: NiTi (nickel-titanium) has shape memory and flexibility — used early. Stainless steel is stiffer, used in final stages. Sizes .012, .014, .016, .018 — increasing stiffness.

cards.q: What's different about calling on orthodontists?
cards.a: They need specialized product knowledge, they see a lot of reps, they buy in volume, and they're brand loyal once established.
cards.n: Harder to get in, but worth more once you're in.

cards.q: Dentsply Sirona owns what?
cards.a:
The largest pure-play dental company (ticker XRAY):
  • Implants — Astra Tech, Ankylos
  • CAD/CAM — CEREC
  • Imaging — Schick sensors
  • Consumables — Prime & Bond, Aquasil, Caulk
  • Endodontics — Maillefer files
  • Orthodontics — SureSmile, TP Orthodontics

cards.q: Envista owns what?
cards.a: Spun off from Danaher: Nobel Biocare (implants), Ormco (orthodontics), KaVo Kerr (handpieces, imaging, endo).
cards.n: Your notes list these under Danaher too — Envista is where they live now.

cards.q: Align Technology owns what?
cards.a: Invisalign (aligners), iTero (scanners), exocad (digital design software). Pure-play digital dentistry.
cards.n: That's why iTero and Invisalign integrate so tightly — same company.

cards.q: Straumann Group owns what?
cards.a: Straumann implants (#1 share), Neodent (value implants), ClearCorrect (aligners), plus digital acquisitions.

cards.q: 3M Health Care owns what?
cards.a: Filtek composites, Scotchbond adhesives, RelyX cements, Unitek orthodontics.

cards.q: Planmeca?
cards.a: Finnish and family-owned. Imaging (pano, CBCT) and CAD/CAM. Known for innovation.
cards.n: Family-owned means no quarterly-earnings pressure — different buying relationship than a public company.

cards.q: How do you research a competitor?
cards.a:
1. Ask practices — "what else are you using?"
  2. Trade shows — Chicago Midwinter, ADA annual
  3. LinkedIn — see where competitors worked
  4. Product catalogs
  5. Clinical studies and publications

cards.q: What goes on a battle card?
cards.a:
1. Price comparison
  2. Feature differences
  3. Clinical evidence
  4. Service and support differences
  5. Why practices choose them
  6. Why practices leave them
cards.n: That last one is the most useful and the one people skip.

questions: Largest dental distributor in the world?
Three names, three slots: Schein, Patterson, Benco. Schein alone is roughly the other two put together.
Roughly what share of the market does Henry Schein hold?
Close to half of everything a dental office orders moves through one company. That's why every Big 3 conversation starts with Schein.
Patterson is the one in the middle - big enough to compete with Schein head-on, which is why they show up against you.
Benco is the smallest of the Big 3 and family-owned. It's the one people forget - and the one your notes had as "Banko."
The distributor is the ___ of a dental office.
A quarterback never scores, but nothing moves until they touch it. Same job: you don't do the dentistry, but everything they use came through you.
How are dental distributor reps mostly employed?
W-2 means these are employees with territories, not gig contractors. It's a career track, and it's why the company invests in training you.
Roughly how many dentist products are out there?
Nobody memorizes 300,000 SKUs - not you, not the dentist. That gap is exactly why they need a rep they trust instead of a catalog.
Which two companies sell dental equipment and technology?
A-dec and Planmeca sell the big hardware - chairs, units, imaging. Different world from consumables: bought rarely, costs a fortune, lasts a decade.
The intraoral scanner is the digital replacement for goopy impressions and film. If an office is buying one, they're modernizing - that opens other doors.
Which implant companies does Henry Schein own?
Schein doesn't just ship other people's implants, it owns two implant brands. Distributor and manufacturer at the same time.
Who are the largest dental manufacturers?
Manufacturers make it, distributors move it. Dentsply Sirona builds the product; Schein puts it on the doorstep. Don't mix the two lists up.
Roughly how many dentists are there in the world?
200,000 worldwide is a small, closed profession. Reputations travel - which is why burning one office actually costs you.
Dental insurance is really more of a:
It's a discount program with an annual cap, usually around ,,000-$2,000. Patients blow through that fast, and everything after is cash out of pocket.
How does Medicaid work in dental?
It doesn't - there's no dental equivalent
The medical safety net just doesn't extend here. No equivalent program means the patient pays or the work doesn't happen.
Which of these is normally out of pocket?
Dentures, crowns and veneers are the high-ticket items insurance barely touches. That's where the case-acceptance conversation lives.
Why does a dentist treat every purchase as personal money?
They make what they charge their patients
The dentist usually owns the practice. Surgeons and physicians draw a salary; a dentist takes home what's left. Every box you sell comes out of their own pocket - price it like you know that.
What does DMD after a name tell you?
DMD or DDS both mean general dentist - the degrees are equivalent. Specialists carry an additional title on top.
Biggest clear aligner company in the game?
Invisalign is the category - people say it the way they say Kleenex. Note the spelling: Invis-align, as in aligning.
Which one is NOT a dental specialist?
The dental specialties: perio (gums), endo (root canals), pedo (kids), ortho (straightening), oral surgery. Cardiology is not on the list.
What are the Big 4 procedure categories?
Implants, preventives, restoratives, endodontics. Learn these as buckets - almost every product you sell drops into one of them.
Front to back, food gets broken down in stages: cut, tear, crush, grind. Incisors are the front blades that start it.
Canines are the pointed ones - think of a dog's fang. Made for tearing, and they have the longest roots in the mouth.
Premolars sit between the tearers and the grinders, and they do the in-between job: crushing.
Molars are the flat millstones at the back. Cut, tear, crush, grind - grinding is the last step before you swallow.
MAXilla = MAX, at the top. It's fixed to the skull and doesn't move.
The mandible is the one that actually moves - your lower jaw is the only bone in your skull with a real joint.
Gingiva is gums - same root as gingivitis, which is literally inflamed gums.
What sits right next to the maxilla?
The sinus sits directly above the upper back teeth. That's why upper implants sometimes need a sinus lift first - there isn't enough bone between.
The inferior alveolar nerve runs through the lower jaw. Hit it and the patient loses feeling in their lip - which is why lower implants get scanned and planned so carefully.
What is the alveolar bone's one job?
Holds the tooth - and shrinks if it's lost
It holds the tooth, and it shrinks once the tooth is gone because nothing is stimulating it anymore. That shrinkage is the entire reason bone grafts get sold alongside implants.
Order it from the jaw out to the tooth:
Jaw bone, alveolar bone, gums, teeth
Gums, jaw bone, teeth, alveolar bone
Teeth, gums, alveolar bone, jaw bone
Alveolar bone, jaw bone, teeth, gums
Work outward from the deepest structure to the one you can see: jaw bone, alveolar bone, gums, teeth.
Are teeth bone, and do they grow back?
Not bone, but they do grow back
Bone has a blood supply and heals; enamel has neither, so damage is permanent. That one fact is why the entire preventive category - fluoride, sealants, restoratives - exists.
Cavities - what does the dentist buy?
Composite filling, bonding agents, fluoride, sealants
Match the product to the problem. Cavities are a restore-and-prevent job: fill what's decayed, then seal and strengthen what isn't.
Periodontal disease - what does the dentist buy?
Perio is a gum and bone problem, so the tools clean below the gumline and rebuild what was lost - scalers, lasers, grafts, antimicrobials.
Crooked teeth - what does the dentist buy?
Straightening runs cheapest to most invasive: braces, aligners, TADs for tough cases, and surgery only when the jaw itself is off.
Losing teeth - what does the dentist buy?
Replacing teeth means replacing the foundation too - which is why grafts sell next to implants. Remember the alveolar bone shrinks once the tooth is gone.
A temporary anchoring device is a mini screw placed as a fixed anchor point to pull teeth against. Temporary - it comes out when the move is done.
Odds the dentist is actually available when you walk in?
Roughly two out of three stops won't get you face time. Plan the route expecting that, and treat the staff as the real relationship.
How many touches before you get consistent calls?
6 to 8. Most reps quit around three and conclude the office isn't interested - the ones who keep going get the calls.
They respond to promos and deals. Lead with what's actually on offer, not a general check-in.
What keeps a dentist calling you back?
Consistency, follow up, doing what you said
Consistency, follow up, and doing what you said you'd do. Cheapest price wins one order; being reliable wins the account.
Central and lateral incisors, top and bottom. Single root, thin edge, built for cutting.
One at each corner of the arch. Also called cuspids or eye teeth.
Also called bicuspids. Bi-cuspid = two cusps, which is literally where the name comes from.
How many molars, wisdom teeth included?
Drops to 8 once the wisdom teeth come out - which is most people.
Which teeth have the longest roots in the mouth?
Longest roots means most stable, which is why canines are the last teeth to be lost.
What does "bicuspid" tell you about a premolar?
Bi = two, cuspid = cusp. The name describes the chewing surface.
How many cusps does a molar have?
Largest teeth in the mouth, 2-3 roots, and the most complex anatomy to work on.
When do the first molars erupt?
They're literally called the 6-year molars. First adult teeth in, and often the first to decay.
In the team analogy, what are the canines?
Incisors are the forwards (visible, aesthetic), premolars the midfielders (transition), molars the power players (heavy lifting).
Which jaw has the densest bone?
Densest at the front of the lower jaw. That density is why it's the best implant location.
Where do teeth move faster in orthodontics?
Thinner maxillary bone moves faster; the dense mandible is slower. Same reason implants behave differently up top.
Why do upper back implants often need a sinus lift?
The maxillary sinus leaves too little bone
The nerve is in the way
Sinus sits right above the upper back teeth. Not enough bone between them means grafting first - which is a sale.
Between the premolars in the lower jaw
In the roof of the mouth
It's where the nerve exits the mandible. Knowing it's there is why imaging gets sold with lower implants.
What do healthy gums look like?
Stippled means a faint orange-peel texture. Diseased gums are red, swollen and bleed easily.
What happens to alveolar bone when a tooth is lost?
Use it or lose it - nothing is stimulating the bone anymore. This is the single most useful fact in implant selling.
How much bone can be lost in the first 3 years after tooth loss?
That speed is why immediate placement and ridge preservation grafts matter - wait and there's nothing to place into.
Strep mutans plus sugar makes acid
Bacteria plus sugar makes acid, acid demineralizes enamel. That's the whole disease process.
Caught at the white spot it's preventive. Reaching the pulp means a root canal - and a very different product list.
Class I caries are found where?
Pits and fissures on chewing surfaces
Class I is the classic sealant target - the grooves on top of molars.
Class V caries are found where?
Class II is between back teeth, Class III between front teeth, Class IV a front corner or edge, Class VI cusp tips.
The probe number is the whole diagnosis. 4mm+ with bone loss is periodontitis.
Gingivitis is gums only and reversible. Once bone is lost it's periodontitis, and that doesn't reverse.
Periodontitis starts at what pocket depth?
4mm+ plus bone loss on the x-ray. Chronic is slow, aggressive is rapid.
Lower jaw too far back - overbite
The buck-teeth look. Division 1 has the front teeth sticking out, Division 2 has them tipped back.
Lower jaw too far forward - underbite
Hardest of the three to treat, and the one most likely to need orthognathic surgery.
Which malocclusion class is most common?
Normal molar relationship, but with crowding or spacing. Most aligner cases live here.
What are the options for complete edentulism?
Partial edentulism gets bridges, partials or implants - and is sorted by Kennedy Classification I-IV.
What happens to someone after losing teeth?
Bone resorption, bite collapse, facial aging
The face structurally changes as bone disappears. It's a functional problem, not a cosmetic one.
Most visible - shade matching, bonding, veneers
Aesthetics drive the sale up front. Also trauma-prone in contact sports, which matters for practices seeing athletes.
Why are molars the sealant and crown category?
Highest decay rate from grooves and pits
Grooves trap food and bacteria. Molars also take the most force, so they crack and get crowned most often.
The upper back, behind the sinus
Dense bone means stability. It also supports implant-retained dentures well.
Pulling premolars makes room to straighten the rest. They're also a common cracked-tooth site.
Arestin is the other name worth knowing - a local antimicrobial for periodontal pockets.
When does a ridge preservation graft go in?
Get ahead of resorption. Bone disappears fast once the tooth is gone, so the graft goes in the same visit.
What's the ROI pitch on periodontal maintenance?
It's recurring revenue for the practice
Sell the business case, not just the product. Perio patients come back on a schedule, forever.
What makes edentulism the big opportunity?
An aging population hitting peak tooth loss
It only affects a few patients
Baby boomers are hitting peak tooth-loss years. Implants, grafts, dentures, digital denture workflow - all of it.
Which is an actual conversation opener from the training?
"What percent of your restorations are composite vs amalgam?"
"Can I speak to whoever does the ordering?"
Good openers get the dentist talking about their own practice instead of your catalog.
What are orthodontists specifically trained to do?
It's the whole specialty. When Invisalign launched it was orthodontist-only for exactly this reason.
If one person in the practice dislikes you, what happens?
Nobody in the practice will deal with you
It has no effect on orders
The staff are extremely tight-knit and word travels instantly. Treat the office manager and assistants like decision makers, because they are.
What should you do right after closing a sale?
Ask when they'll use it and follow up after
Move straight to the next account
Put the date in your calendar and text them to ask how it went. Costs nothing and turns a transaction into a relationship.
Which orthodontic items are the repeat business?
Wires, ligature rings and rubber bands
Brackets are bonded on and painful to change, so they're the hard sell. Sell what gets replaced.
What's the difference between inside and outside reps?
Inside works the phones, outside works the territory
Inside sells equipment, outside sells consumables
Inside is salaried, outside is commission
Inside is straight cold calls. Outside drives the area and walks into practices.
What share of a practice's spend goes to supplies?
It's a small slice of their budget - which is exactly why convenience and reliability often beat price.
What share of consumables runs through full-service dealers?
Henry Schein, Patterson and Benco. The other 20% is manufacturer-direct and discounters.
How many practices does a dealer rep typically manage?
That headcount is why time management and routing matter as much as selling.
Price-focused, no service. A real threat to the traditional model.
How do you compete against a discounter?
You cannot win a race to the bottom against Amazon, so don't enter it. Sell the things they can't ship.
Is price the number one driver for consumables?
No - reliability and convenience often beat it
"I need it tomorrow, can you deliver?" wins more accounts than being cheapest.
What do you do on a weekly or bi-weekly visit?
Check inventory, take orders, handle issues
Also introduce new products and gather intel on what they're buying elsewhere. Contracts and capital are monthly and quarterly conversations.
Which metrics do you track on an account?
Volume, product mix, growth rate, order size
Product mix - your brand vs competitors - is the one that tells you whether you're actually winning the account.
What's the manufacturer-direct advantage over a dealer rep?
You're the expert on your own product
The dealer rep is a generalist across 10,000+ SKUs. Depth is the thing you have that they don't.
What's the price range on capital equipment?
And decisions take months, not days, with multiple stakeholders and financing almost always involved.
What's the athletic parallel for a capital sale?
Long courtship, big investment, transformative impact, and everyone weighs in on the decision.
What do intraoral sensor sizes 0, 1 and 2 mean?
Size 0 for kids, 1 for front teeth, 2 for back teeth.
What does an intraoral sensor cost per operatory?
Sales cycle is short for capital - 2 to 4 months.

It's becoming standard of care. Lets them keep surgical cases in-house instead of referring them out.
What does a practice charge for a CBCT scan?

What does an intraoral scanner cost?

What does a complete CEREC system cost?
Scanner plus design software plus milling unit. Ceramic blocks run $30-80 each on top.
Because it eliminates $150-300 in lab fees per crown. That's the whole ROI conversation.
What's the main clinical selling point of CEREC?
Same-day crowns - no temporaries, no second visit

What do soft tissue lasers cost?
Diode is the most common type. Frenectomies, gingivectomies, crown lengthening. Biolase, AMD, Fotona.
What can a hard tissue laser do that a soft tissue laser can't?

Which autoclave class is most thorough?

Regulatory compliance - it's required by law
Then cycle time and reliability - downtime means they literally cannot practice. Replacement cycle is 7-10 years.
What does a dental chair cost?
A-dec is premium, then Midmark and Forest. Usually tied to a renovation, and financing is almost always required.
How fast does a high-speed handpiece turn?
That's "the drill." Slow-speed runs 20,000 RPM for prophy angles and adjustments.
Why does a practice keep 2 to 4 handpieces per operatory?
One's in use while another is being sterilized. $800-3,000 each, so it's real money.
Why is compressor reliability so critical?
The whole operatory stops. $3,000-30,000, sized by number of chairs.
How big is the implant market?
Driven by boomers losing teeth, implants becoming standard of care, more GPs placing them, and success rates above 95%.
What are the three parts of an implant?
Fixture is the screw in the bone, abutment connects, crown is what you see.
What diameters do implant fixtures come in?
Lengths run 6mm to 18mm. Platform comes mini, regular or wide.
TiUnite is Nobel Biocare, Osseospeed is Astra Tech, Laser-Lok is BioHorizons. Surface treatment is what drives osseointegration.
Swiss precision, premium pricing, deep evidence base. Roxolid is their titanium-zirconium alloy.
What does a premium implant cost the dentist, and what do they charge?
That spread is exactly why cost usually isn't the surgeon's first question.
Who invented the modern dental implant?
Nobel Biocare are the pioneers. All-on-4 - a full arch on four implants - is their trademark protocol.
A full arch restored on four implants
Nobel Biocare's trademark protocol, and a major option for complete edentulism.
What do value implant brands cost?
Hiossen, MegaGen, Dentium. The controversy is quality vs cost; the opportunity is price-sensitive practices and high-volume DSOs.
How long is the implant sales cycle?
Awareness, education, trial, conversion, loyalty. Lunch-and-learn to CE course to a few supported cases.
Why are implant systems so hard to switch?
Add the learning curve and compatibility issues. Hard to win an account - very hard to lose one.
Is cost the top decision factor for implant surgeons?
No - outcomes, ease of use and support come first
Clinical outcomes, ease of use, prosthetic flexibility, your availability, and the evidence base. Don't lead with price.
What are the four graft types?
Self, human donor, animal, synthetic. Auto, allo, xeno, allo-plast.
Which graft is the gold standard, and what's the catch?
Autograft - but it needs a second surgical site
The patient's own bone integrates best, but harvesting it from chin, jaw or hip adds morbidity.
LifeNet, MTF, AlloSource. $100-500 per case. Popular because there's no second surgical site.
Geistlich, bovine-derived. Acts as a scaffold and resorbs slowly, so it maintains volume. $150-400.
What's the advantage of a synthetic graft?
Unlimited supply, no disease transmission risk
Alloplast - hydroxyapatite and calcium phosphate. Novabone, Cerasorb.
What does a barrier membrane do?
Covers the graft to guide tissue regeneration

Every extraction is a potential graft

What does an Invisalign case cost the dentist vs the patient?
The dentist submits cases and pays per case, so it scales with their volume.
How many hours a day must a patient wear aligners?

What software plans an Invisalign case?
Digital scan, then AI treatment planning, then aligners manufactured centrally and shipped to the practice.

Which wire is used in the early stages of treatment?

What's true about calling on orthodontists?
They see a lot of reps and are brand loyal once established

Which is the largest pure-play dental company?
Ticker XRAY. Astra Tech and Ankylos implants, CEREC, Schick sensors, Maillefer endo files, SureSmile orthodontics.
Envista was spun off from Danaher and took those brands with it - your notes list them under both.
Same company owning both the aligner and the scanner is why iTero integration is the whole iTero pitch.
Premium implants, value implants, and aligners - they cover the price spectrum deliberately.
Composites, adhesives, cements and orthodontics - all inside a much larger conglomerate.
Imaging and CAD/CAM, known for innovation. No quarterly-earnings pressure means a different kind of buying relationship.

Chicago Midwinter and the ADA annual
Plus asking practices what else they're using, LinkedIn research, catalogs and clinical studies.
